stories.headline: AP moves to capture flood surge as reservoirs gain 21 TMC
stories.title: AP moves to capture flood surge as reservoirs gain 21 TMC
stories.summary: Naidu seeks Centre’s nod for new barrages Orders maximum diversion of rising river flows 29 reservoirs across state record sharp gains Vamsadhara, Nagavali, Godavari, Krishna in spate Announces 50 kg free rice for affected fishermen
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Amaravati: The state government is moving to capture the surge in river flows triggered by heavy rains, with storage in 29 reservoirs rising by about 21 TMC in three days even as several districts face inundation and crop damage.

Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu, who reviewed the flood and rainfall situation with senior officials through a teleconference on Saturday, directed the authorities to make maximum use of the additional water while continuing relief and rescue operations.
The combined storage in 29 reservoirs increased from 101 TMC on September 23 by around 21 TMC by September 26.

Of this, 11 projects in North Andhra gained about 5 TMC, while 18 reservoirs in Kakinada, Polavaram, Alluri Sitarama Raju, Eluru, Palnadu, Nellore, Kurnool, Kadapa and Anantapur districts recorded another 16 TMC.
The sharpest increases were reported in North Andhra.
Inflows into Gotta Barrage in the Vamsadhara basin rose from 7,214 cusecs on September 20 to 47,100 cusecs on September 25.

At Narayanapuram Anicut in the Nagavali basin, inflows surged from 2,100 to 49,800 cusecs, while Madduvvalasa Project saw inflows rise from 918 to nearly 18,000 cusecs, lifting storage from 1.61 TMC to 2.79 TMC.
Inflows at Thotapalli Barrage increased from 2,484 to about 23,250 cusecs.
In the Godavari basin, Donkarayi storage rose from 11.67 TMC to 15.78 TMC and Seeleru reservoir storage from 1.52 TMC to 3.90 TMC.
Dowleswaram flows increased from 1.20 lakh to 3.50 lakh cusecs.
In the Krishna basin, Prakasam Barrage inflows rose from 8,187 to 40,521 cusecs, while Munneru flows increased from 3,210 to 9,000 cusecs.
Naidu directed officials to fill small and medium water bodies wherever possible and to divert available water into reservoirs.

stories.headline: Flood Fury In State: Fields under water, villages cut off
stories.title: Flood Fury In State: Fields under water, villages cut off
stories.summary: Crops in 43,803 hectares inundated across 12 districts 69,258 farmers in 1,216 villages may lose standing crops Nagavali blankets Srikakulam farmlands with a vast sheet of water
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Amaravati: For thousands of families across Andhra Pradesh, the current flooding is no longer just a story of swollen rivers and overflowing fields; it represents the loss of months of labour, livelihoods, and the destruction of hard-won harvest on which they had pinned their hopes.

Farmers who struggled through inadequate rainfall during the Kharif season are now watching standing crops disappear under floodwater, while families in river-island and low-lying villages are finding roads and access routes cut off.
The scale of the calamity is discernible in the preliminary assessment.

Heavy rains and floods have inundated 43,802.83 hectares of agricultural land across 12 districts, affecting 69,258 farmers in 1,216 villages spread over 185 mandals, according to the Preliminary Crop Damage Report as of September 26.
The loss on the farm front is particularly stark in Srikakulam, where the Nagavali has spilled far beyond its banks.
An inflow of about 70,000 cusecs pushed floodwater across thousands of acres, with water carpeting nearly 20 km.
In several fields, there is knee-deep water.
Around 15 villages, including Korlakota, Chimalavalasa and Kothapeta, have vast stretches of paddy under water, while roads connecting villages have also been submerged.
For these farmers, the disaster has come after an already difficult season.
The source report records that they had struggled initially with inadequate rainfall and water availability and had managed to raise the Kharif crop with difficulty.
Now, with the crop approaching harvest, floodwaters have wiped out the results of herculean efforts.
Farmers in Amudalavalasa are seeking immediate field inspections and compensation, with several villages reporting completely submerged fields.

stories.headline: Election panel backs Form 6 for SIR, says SC upheld its use
stories.title: Election panel backs Form 6 for SIR, says SC upheld its use
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: EC retains mandatory SIR declaration for fresh voter enrolment.

NEW DELHI: Those applying for fresh enrolment as electors through Form 6 in locations other than the 12 states and UTs where special intensive revision (SIR) is currently underway will no longer need to attach a declaration mapping themselves or their relative to the electoral rolls from the last SIR.

In the states and UTs where SIR is going on, Form 6 will continue to be accompanied by a mandatory declaration by the applicant listing their or their relatives' electoral rolls details from the last SIR, apart from their father's, mother's and spouse's names and their respective EPIC numbers, if available.

A statement put out by the three-member Election Commission Saturday justified the continued requirement of new electors to submit the declaration along with Form 6 as part of SIR, saying "the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR has been upheld by the Supreme Court".
For the non-SIR period, the forms applicable as per the Registration of Electors Rules 1960 will be used, the commission added.
The declaration was first added to Form 6 in the SIR order issued for Bihar on June 24, 2025.
Sources told TOI the system will revert to the pre-SIR Form 6 with immediate effect in non-SIR states/UTs, including the states due for polls early next year.
As exclusively reported by TOI on Sept 25, a special summary revision will be undertaken in these poll-bound states later this year.

Both election commissioners, SS Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had in May and Aug, respectively, sent internal notes to the deputy election commissioner concerned, opining that Form 6 can only be amended by the govt.
This was after they had approved of the declaration attached to the form as part of three SIR orders.
While election commissioner Vivek Joshi raised objection to the revised Form 6 format on May 16 this year, Sandhu endorsed it on Aug 13, well after Supreme Court had upheld the SIR process.
Their concerns were later echoed by opposition parties led by Congress, which alleged that Form 6 was changed "unilaterally" by CEC Gyanesh Kumar.

stories.headline: Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi | Dissent in the Election Commission
stories.title: Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi | Dissent in the Election Commission
stories.summary: The two Election Commissioner, both appointed by the government under the new 2023 law, have raised questions about changes to electoral rolls, centralised control and the Election Commission’s decision-making process
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: When notices began to be issued after the publication of the draft list during the Delhi SIR [special intensive revision], one of the names was that of Election Commissioner (EC) Sukhbir Singh Sandhu.

What was considered ironical on that day and time soon became a moment of reckoning for the poll body as reports emerged that Dr. Sandhu, along with his fellow Election Commissioner Vivek Joshi, had flagged many anomalies in the ongoing SIR process across the country over the last 10 months.

Though rumours of a rift within the Election Commission of India had been doing the rounds for some months, what came as a surprise were the formal dissent notes written by the two ECs, including one to the Cabinet Secretary, as both had been virtually handpicked by the government under the new 2023 Law for Appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners.
The Opposition Congress party had given written objections during the appointment of both in the selection committee meetings.

When Dr. Sandhu was appointed along with CEC Gyanesh Kumar on March 14, 2024, following the retirement of EC Anup Chandra Pandey and the abrupt resignation of EC Arun Goel, Congress leader Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury had given a formal dissent note in the selection committee.
Later, when Mr. Joshi was appointed on February 17, 2025 after Gyanesh Kumar was elevated to CEC, Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi raised objection in the committee meeting.
Both the Election Commissioners had reportedly flagged several key issues, including the centralisation of the Electoral Rolls.
In May this year, Mr. Joshi proposed an audit to certify that “no one except the concerned statutory authorities has any credentials to make any change in the (voter) database”.

In August, Dr. Sandhu recorded that State-level election officials were reporting that they do not have “proper and complete access” to the ERONet portal — the digital system through which the electoral rolls are maintained.

He further flagged that Election Commission Director General of IT “does not have any legal authority to restrict proper and complete access and freedom to operate as given by law to the statutory authorities”.
The two ECs also said that Form 6 — which new voters must fill to register— was altered to ask if the applicant or their parents/grandparents “exist” in the electoral roll of the last SIR.

They warned as early as May that such a statutory form cannot be changed without amending the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, and Dr. Sandhu called the change “unauthorised and illegal” in August, demanding its immediate removal.

stories.headline: Saving Kashmir’s Wetlands Is Saving Our Future
stories.title: Saving Kashmir’s Wetlands Is Saving Our Future
stories.summary: Kashmir’s wetlands are often noticed only when they become scenic backdrops, birdwatching destinations or the subject of an occasional official celebration. Yet these fragile water bodies are far more than picturesque remnants of a landscape people once knew better. They are among the Valley’s most important natural systems—quietly storing floodwater, recharging groundwater, filtering pollution, supporting agriculture and sustaining a remarkable variety of birds, fish and plant life. Their decline should therefore concern every resident of Kashmir, not only environmentalists. When a wetland shrinks, is filled with debris or is cut off from its natural channels, the loss is not confined to birds and reeds. It weakens the Valley’s capacity to absorb heavy rainfall, increases the pressure on rivers and drainage networks, damages livelihoods and reduces the ecological resilience of communities already facing rapid urbanisation and a changing climate. The crisis is visible across the Valley. Wetlands have been narrowed by encroachments, fragmented by roads and construction, choked by solid waste and contaminated by untreated sewage. Water channels that once connected lakes, marshes and agricultural fields have been blocked or diverted. In several places, the boundary between wetland and settlement has become a matter of dispute rather than a clearly protected ecological limit. Each unauthorised filling may appear small, but together these interventions are eroding a system that took centuries to evolve. The consequences are particularly serious in a region vulnerable to floods. Kashmir’s wetlands function as natural sponges. During periods of intense rainfall or snowmelt, they hold excess water and release it gradually. This reduces the speed and volume of runoff entering rivers and populated areas. When these holding areas are lost, water has fewer places to go. Drains overflow more quickly, low-lying settlements face greater risk, and the burden on embankments and engineered flood-control structures increases. This natural protection is often undervalued because it does not arrive in the form of a government project or a concrete structure. But a healthy wetland can provide a service that would otherwise require expensive engineering, regular maintenance and substantial public money. Destroying such a system and then trying to replace it with pumps, walls and drains is not development. It is an expensive admission that nature was treated as disposable. Wetlands also help regulate the Valley’s water cycle. They absorb and store water, contribute to groundwater recharge and improve the quality of water by trapping sediments and absorbing some pollutants. This function becomes increasingly important as settlements expand and demand for water rises. A wetland that is polluted or disconnected from its catchment cannot perform these services effectively. Its deterioration eventually affects farms, households and downstream ecosystems. The ecological value of Kashmir’s wetlands is equally significant. The Valley lies along important migratory routes and attracts birds from distant parts of Asia and beyond. Wetlands such as Hokersar, Haigam, Shallabugh and other marshes provide feeding and resting grounds for migratory waterfowl. Their seasonal arrival is not merely a spectacle. It is evidence that these ecosystems remain connected to wider natural processes. When birds stop arriving in the same numbers, or when they find less food and shelter, the warning is ecological as well as symbolic. It indicates that water quality, vegetation, fish populations or safe resting areas may be declining. The loss of biodiversity also weakens the health of the ecosystem. Every species has a role in the food chain, nutrient cycle and regeneration of habitat. The disappearance of wetlands would also damage the Valley’s cultural memory. Kashmir’s relationship with water has always been intimate. Rivers, springs, lakes and marshes have shaped settlement, agriculture, transport, folklore and everyday life. Wetlands formed part of the seasonal rhythm of rural communities. They supported grazing, fishing, reed collection and farming. To lose them is to lose not only habitat but also a part of the landscape through which generations understood their home. Yet environmental protection in Kashmir often remains reactive. Authorities act after encroachment becomes visible, after a flood exposes a drainage failure or after public concern grows over pollution. By then, restoration is more difficult and far more costly. The priority must shift from occasional rescue to continuous protection. The first requirement is an accurate and publicly accessible inventory of wetlands. Boundaries should be mapped scientifically, updated regularly and marked clearly on the ground. Satellite imagery, local surveys and community testimony can together help identify changes in wetland area, water flow and land use. Without a reliable baseline, it is difficult to determine whether a wetland is shrinking, who is responsible or whether restoration measures are working. Legal protection must then be matched by enforcement. A wetland cannot be protected on paper while construction, dumping or land filling continues around it. Agencies responsible for revenue, planning, housing, irrigation, drainage and environment must work from the same maps and share accountability. There should be no room for contradictory permissions, delayed action or administrative ambiguity. At the same time, enforcement must distinguish between deliberate commercial encroachment and the needs of communities that have lived around wetlands for generations. People dependent on fishing, agriculture, grazing or collection of reeds should not be treated as environmental offenders by default. Conservation will succeed only when local residents see wetlands as protected commons that support their future, not as obstacles to development or threats to their livelihoods. This requires community participation in a meaningful form. Local committees can help monitor dumping, report encroachments, track changes in water levels and support seasonal protection of bird habitats. Schools and colleges can participate in wetland watch programmes, bird counts and water-quality monitoring. Such initiatives should not be reduced to ceremonial clean-up drives. They must be linked to scientific data and official decision-making. Pollution control is another urgent priority. Untreated sewage, plastic waste, agricultural runoff and construction debris are steadily reducing the capacity of wetlands to sustain life. Cleaning visible waste is useful but insufficient. The sources of pollution must be identified and controlled. Sewage treatment facilities need to function reliably, drains must be monitored and waste disposal rules must be enforced. A wetland cannot be restored if pollution continues to enter it from upstream. The wider catchment must also be considered. A wetland is not an isolated water body with a line around it. Its health depends on the streams, drains, springs, fields and slopes that feed it. If a channel is blocked or concretised upstream, the wetland may receive too little water. If soil is washed down from construction sites, it may become shallow and silted. If pesticides and sewage enter the catchment, the wetland becomes a reservoir of contamination. Restoration plans must therefore be based on hydrology rather than beautification. Removing silt may be necessary in some areas, but indiscriminate dredging can destroy vegetation and breeding grounds. Planting ornamental species along a wetland edge may improve its appearance while harming its ecological character. Concrete walkways, lighting and commercial facilities can fragment habitat and disturb birds. A restored wetland should be judged by its ecological function, not by how attractive it looks in a photograph. Urban planning must also change. The Valley’s towns are expanding rapidly, often into low-lying and water-sensitive areas. Master plans should identify wetlands, floodplains and natural drainage channels as no-build zones. Roads and housing projects must be assessed for their impact on water flow before construction begins. Development cannot be called sustainable if it creates flood risk for the very communities it is meant to serve. Climate change makes this task even more urgent. Changes in rainfall patterns, warmer winters, irregular snowfall and intense precipitation events are already altering the Valley’s hydrology. Wetlands provide a buffer against such uncertainty. They cannot prevent every flood or drought, but they can reduce vulnerability. Protecting them is therefore an essential part of climate adaptation, not a luxury reserved for times when other problems have been solved. The economic argument for conservation is strong as well. Wetlands support agriculture, fisheries, tourism, research and local employment. They reduce the cost of flood damage, water treatment and artificial drainage. Bird tourism, if managed responsibly, can create income for surrounding communities without destroying habitat. But economic use must remain within ecological limits. A wetland that is overbuilt, overvisited or polluted will eventually lose the very qualities that attract visitors and generate income. What is needed now is not another declaration of concern but a Valley-wide wetland action plan with clear targets, timelines and responsibility. It should identify priority wetlands, publish their boundaries, measure water quality, restore natural channels, remove major pollution sources and establish a transparent system for reporting violations. Progress should be reviewed publicly, and local communities should have access to the information. The government has an important role, but responsibility does not end there. Citizens must stop treating wetlands as dumping grounds or vacant land. Builders and businesses must recognise that short-term gains from illegal filling impose long-term costs on society. Political representatives must resist the temptation to support encroachments for immediate popularity. Courts, civil society, researchers and the media must continue to draw attention to violations and demand accountability. Kashmir’s wetlands are not empty spaces waiting to be converted. They are living infrastructure, natural archives and shared inheritance. They protect towns, nourish fields, host migratory birds and preserve the ecological balance of the Valley. Once destroyed, they cannot be recreated simply by digging a new pond or planting a few saplings. The choice before Kashmir is clear. It can continue to allow wetlands to disappear through gradual neglect, fragmented permissions and weak enforcement, or it can treat them as essential public assets deserving serious investment and protection. Saving them will require patience, science, law and community participation. But the cost of inaction will be far greater. To save the wetlands is to save the Valley’s water, biodiversity, memories and future. That is not an environmental slogan. It is a public necessity. (The author is a research scholar and freelancer)

People dependent on fishing, agriculture, grazing or collection of reeds should not be treated as environmental offenders by default.
Conservation will succeed only when local residents see wetlands as protected commons that support their future, not as obstacles to development or threats to their livelihoods.
This requires community participation in a meaningful form.
Local committees can help monitor dumping, report encroachments, track changes in water levels and support seasonal protection of bird habitats.
Schools and colleges can participate in wetland watch programmes, bird counts and water-quality monitoring.
Such initiatives should not be reduced to ceremonial clean-up drives.
They must be linked to scientific data and official decision-making.
Pollution control is another urgent priority.
Untreated sewage, plastic waste, agricultural runoff and construction debris are steadily reducing the capacity of wetlands to sustain life.
Cleaning visible waste is useful but insufficient.
The sources of pollution must be identified and controlled.
Sewage treatment facilities need to function reliably, drains must be monitored and waste disposal rules must be enforced.
A wetland cannot be restored if pollution continues to enter it from upstream.
The wider catchment must also be considered.
A wetland is not an isolated water body with a line around it.
Its health depends on the streams, drains, springs, fields and slopes that feed it.
If a channel is blocked or concretised upstream, the wetland may receive too little water.
If soil is washed down from construction sites, it may become shallow and silted.
If pesticides and sewage enter the catchment, the wetland becomes a reservoir of contamination.
Restoration plans must therefore be based on hydrology rather than beautification.
Removing silt may be necessary in some areas, but indiscriminate dredging can destroy vegetation and breeding grounds.
Planting ornamental species along a wetland edge may improve its appearance while harming its ecological character.
Concrete walkways, lighting and commercial facilities can fragment habitat and disturb birds.
A restored wetland should be judged by its ecological function, not by how attractive it looks in a photograph.
Urban planning must also change.
The Valley’s towns are expanding rapidly, often into low-lying and water-sensitive areas.
Master plans should identify wetlands, floodplains and natural drainage channels as no-build zones.
Roads and housing projects must be assessed for their impact on water flow before construction begins.
Development cannot be called sustainable if it creates flood risk for the very communities it is meant to serve.
Climate change makes this task even more urgent.
Changes in rainfall patterns, warmer winters, irregular snowfall and intense precipitation events are already altering the Valley’s hydrology.
Wetlands provide a buffer against such uncertainty.
They cannot prevent every flood or drought, but they can reduce vulnerability.
Protecting them is therefore an essential part of climate adaptation, not a luxury reserved for times when other problems have been solved.
The economic argument for conservation is strong as well.
Wetlands support agriculture, fisheries, tourism, research and local employment.
They reduce the cost of flood damage, water treatment and artificial drainage.
Bird tourism, if managed responsibly, can create income for surrounding communities without destroying habitat.
But economic use must remain within ecological limits.
A wetland that is overbuilt, overvisited or polluted will eventually lose the very qualities that attract visitors and generate income.
What is needed now is not another declaration of concern but a Valley-wide wetland action plan with clear targets, timelines and responsibility.

It should identify priority wetlands, publish their boundaries, measure water quality, restore natural channels, remove major pollution sources and establish a transparent system for reporting violations.
Progress should be reviewed publicly, and local communities should have access to the information.
The government has an important role, but responsibility does not end there.
Citizens must stop treating wetlands as dumping grounds or vacant land.
Builders and businesses must recognise that short-term gains from illegal filling impose long-term costs on society.
Political representatives must resist the temptation to support encroachments for immediate popularity.
Courts, civil society, researchers and the media must continue to draw attention to violations and demand accountability.
Kashmir’s wetlands are not empty spaces waiting to be converted.
They are living infrastructure, natural archives and shared inheritance.
They protect towns, nourish fields, host migratory birds and preserve the ecological balance of the Valley.
Once destroyed, they cannot be recreated simply by digging a new pond or planting a few saplings.
The choice before Kashmir is clear.

It can continue to allow wetlands to disappear through gradual neglect, fragmented permissions and weak enforcement, or it can treat them as essential public assets deserving serious investment and protection.
Saving them will require patience, science, law and community participation.
But the cost of inaction will be far greater.
To save the wetlands is to save the Valley’s water, biodiversity, memories and future.
That is not an environmental slogan.
It is a public necessity.
(The author is a research scholar and freelancer).

stories.headline: Autonomy Resolution — Engine of Separatism
stories.title: Autonomy Resolution — Engine of Separatism
stories.summary: The renewed invocation of the Jammu and Kashmir Autonomy Resolution of 2000 raises a question far larger than the immediate political debate over restoration of statehood. It brings back into public discourse an older constitutional idea—the restoration of a distinctive constitutional relationship between Jammu and Kashmir and the Union of India associated broadly with the pre-1953 position. That debate cannot, however, be conducted in 2026 as though the constitutional developments of August 2019 and the judgment of the Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court delivered on 11 December 2023 never occurred. The historical criticism of the autonomy project has been that, even when presented as autonomy within India rather than separation from India, its architecture emphasised constitutional separateness. Its critics therefore saw autonomy as providing political and institutional space in which a consciousness of separateness could survive and potentially strengthen separatist narratives. Supporters of autonomy strongly dispute that interpretation. The National Conference has historically maintained that autonomy was sought within the Indian Union. That distinction must be acknowledged. Advocacy of autonomy is not, merely by itself, legally synonymous with advocacy of secession. The real question today is consequently more precise: Can the political concept underlying the Autonomy Resolution of 2000 simply be revived after Parliament fundamentally changed J&K's constitutional position in 2019 and the Supreme Court subsequently upheld the central constitutional outcome of those changes? Autonomy Was Never Merely Administrative Decentralisation There is a fundamental difference between decentralisation and the historical autonomy demand in Jammu and Kashmir. Every State within the Indian constitutional system possesses legislative and executive powers distributed under the Constitution. States frequently demand greater fiscal authority, increased administrative discretion and greater participation in decisions taken by the Union. Such demands form an ordinary part of Indian federal politics. The National Conference's historical autonomy project went considerably further. The 2000 resolution sought restoration of a constitutional arrangement broadly associated with the position existing before 9 August 1953. The political significance of the demand therefore lay in seeking restoration of a degree of constitutional distinctiveness that had progressively diminished as provisions of the Constitution of India were extended to Jammu and Kashmir. This is precisely why autonomy became inseparable from the wider political debate concerning J&K's relationship with the Union. The controversy was never merely about whether Srinagar or New Delhi should exercise a particular administrative power. It concerned the nature of the constitutional relationship itself. For critics of the autonomy project, that distinction was crucial. They argued that continuously presenting Jammu and Kashmir's relationship with India as constitutionally exceptional could reinforce a psychology of separateness. For supporters of autonomy, precisely the opposite was true: recognition of J&K's distinct history and identity, they argued, could accommodate regional aspirations within India. These competing narratives shaped J&K politics for decades. From Accession to Constitutional Integration Jammu and Kashmir unquestionably possessed an unusual constitutional history. Article 370 provided the constitutional mechanism through which provisions of the Constitution of India were progressively applied to the erstwhile State. Over several decades, numerous provisions of the Indian Constitution were extended to Jammu and Kashmir through Presidential Orders. Two fundamentally different interpretations emerged from this process. Those favouring greater integration regarded these developments as the gradual constitutional integration of Jammu and Kashmir with the rest of India. Autonomy advocates frequently described the same process as an erosion of the constitutional arrangement originally envisaged for the State. The 2000 Autonomy Resolution must be understood against this background. Its objective was not simply greater administrative efficiency or financial decentralisation. It sought substantial restoration of an earlier constitutional position. This raised the fundamental question that dominated J&K's constitutional politics: Should Jammu and Kashmir maintain a uniquely distinctive constitutional relationship with India, or should it function substantially within the same constitutional framework applicable throughout the Union? It was within this contest that the autonomy-versus-integration debate developed. The Connection With Separatist Politics The word “separatism” needs to be used carefully. Separatism in its strict legal and political sense involves seeking separation from the sovereign State. The National Conference's declared position has historically been that its autonomy programme contemplated Jammu and Kashmir remaining within India. Autonomy therefore cannot automatically be equated with secession. The historical criticism is nevertheless important. Critics of the autonomy model argue that separateness can exist without formal separation. A separate constitutional arrangement, exceptional political institutions, restrictions upon the ordinary application of Union laws and a continuing discourse portraying J&K's relationship with India as fundamentally different from that of other States could, in this view, provide an intellectual and political environment in which ideas of distinct political identity could flourish. It is in this sense that critics describe autonomy as an “engine of separatism.” The argument is not necessarily that everybody demanding autonomy seeks independence. Such a proposition would be both historically and legally overbroad. The argument is instead that constitutional exceptionalism can reinforce a political consciousness of exceptionalism, which separatist movements may then seek to exploit. Whether autonomy reduces alienation through accommodation or reinforces separateness through exceptionalism has long been one of the central disagreements in J&K politics. August 2019 Fundamentally Changed the Debate Whatever arguments could legitimately be advanced before August 2019, the constitutional landscape thereafter changed fundamentally. On 5 August 2019, the Union Government initiated constitutional measures that ultimately resulted in Article 370 ceasing to operate in its previous form. The constitutional arrangement through which Article 35A had operated also came to an end. Parliament simultaneously enacted the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, reorganising the former State into the Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh. The importance of these developments cannot be understated. The earlier autonomy debate operated inside the constitutional architecture created by Article 370. The 2000 Autonomy Resolution could therefore proceed from the existence of that constitutional architecture and argue about how the relationship between J&K and the Union should operate within it. After 2019, that premise fundamentally changed. The constitutional mechanism upon which the historical autonomy programme depended no longer operates in its previous form. Political language developed in 2000 therefore cannot simply be transplanted into the constitutional environment of 2026. Parliament Cannot Be Ignored Another aspect of the post-2019 position is equally significant. The transformation was not simply the result of an executive announcement. Parliament acted. The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019, was enacted by Parliament and fundamentally altered the institutional structure of the former State. The present Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir functions within that statutory framework. This becomes particularly significant when examining the authority of the present Legislative Assembly. Section 13 of the Reorganisation Act makes Article 239A of the Constitution applicable to the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir. Section 14 provides for a Legislative Assembly for the Union Territory. The present Assembly is consequently not the legislature of the erstwhile State continuing under the old pre-2019 arrangement. Its immediate statutory structure arises from the parliamentary legislation forming part of the post-2019 constitutional reorganisation. That produces an extraordinary feature of the present debate: The legislature functioning under the post-2019 framework is being used as a political forum to preserve reference to an autonomy resolution whose objective was restoration of a constitutional arrangement preceding that very framework. There is nothing inherently impermissible about legislators debating constitutional change. Democratic institutions exist precisely for political discussion. But the distinction between the right to advocate change and the constitutional authority to accomplish that change becomes decisive. The Supreme Court Judgment Cannot Be Wished Away The next constitutional milestone came on 11 December 2023. A five-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court delivered its judgment in In Re: Article 370 of the Constitution. The judgment fundamentally altered the terms upon which any contemporary autonomy argument must proceed. The Supreme Court held that Article 370 was intended to be a temporary provision. It upheld the central constitutional outcome through which Article 370 ceased to operate in its earlier form. Even more significantly for the historical autonomy debate, the Court rejected the proposition that Jammu and Kashmir retained an element of internal sovereignty distinct from India after accession. This conclusion strikes at an important constitutional premise underlying arguments which portray J&K's relationship with India as a continuing relationship between two repositories of sovereignty. Once the Supreme Court has held that Jammu and Kashmir possessed no residual internal sovereignty separate from India, any future arrangement concerning J&K must necessarily derive its authority from the Constitution of India. Autonomy cannot therefore be asserted as an independent sovereign entitlement existing outside the Constitution. Any constitutional restructuring must proceed through constitutionally competent institutions and constitutionally recognised procedures. It should equally be acknowledged that the Supreme Court did not approve every technique used during the 2019 process. It held that Article 367 could not be employed indirectly to amend Article 370 in the particular manner attempted through part of C.O. 272. Nevertheless, the Court upheld the substantive exercise of power under Article 370(3) and the ultimate constitutional result. That distinction matters. The constitutional outcome of 2019 survived scrutiny by India's highest constitutional court. What Can the Present Assembly Actually Achieve? This brings us to the central institutional question. The present J&K Legislative Assembly can debate. It can pass resolutions. It can articulate political aspirations. It can demand restoration of statehood. It can request the Union Government to take particular actions. It can urge Parliament to reconsider existing legislation. Its members and political parties can advocate future constitutional amendments. But an Assembly resolution cannot, by itself, restore Article 370. It cannot revive Article 35A. It cannot override an Act of Parliament. It cannot independently recreate the pre-1953 constitutional relationship. And it cannot nullify a constitutional position which has already undergone adjudication before a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court. The question facing anybody seeking revival of the 2000 autonomy arrangement is therefore straightforward: Under what existing provision of the Constitution, and through which constitutionally competent institution, is the pre-1953 arrangement proposed to be restored? Unless that question is answered, the autonomy resolution remains primarily a political declaration rather than an instrument possessing independent constitutional capacity to change J&K's present status. Statehood Is Not Autonomy Another distinction is particularly important in the contemporary debate. Restoration of statehood and restoration of the pre-2019 special constitutional position are not the same thing. Jammu and Kashmir can theoretically regain statehood without restoration of Article 370 or Article 35A. Indeed, the Supreme Court's 2023 judgment recorded the Solicitor General's statement that statehood would be restored to Jammu and Kashmir. Statehood therefore remains a distinct constitutional and political question. That makes the continuing invocation of the 2000 Autonomy Resolution particularly worthy of scrutiny. If the immediate political objective is restoration of statehood, why must a resolution seeking statehood preserve reference to the old autonomy demand? The National Conference's position can be understood as maintaining continuity with its longstanding political programme. Its opponents can legitimately argue that restoration of statehood should not be conflated with revival of a pre-2019 special-status agenda. The two propositions have entirely different constitutional consequences. The Constitutional Paradox There is therefore a striking paradox. The present Assembly exists within the post-2019 constitutional and statutory arrangement. The authority under which it functions is part of the very institutional framework created after the constitutional transformation that the historical autonomy programme sought, in important respects, to avoid or reverse. Yet that Assembly is now a forum in which the political relevance of the 2000 autonomy formula is being preserved. This may be politically permissible. But political symbolism cannot substitute for constitutional authority. A legislature cannot acquire power merely by passing a resolution asserting an objective outside its legislative competence. Nor can an Assembly resolution supersede Parliament or undo a constitutional position upheld by the Supreme Court. Why 2019 Must Be the New Constitutional Starting Point The most important weakness in attempts to revive the old autonomy discourse is therefore not political but constitutional. Jammu and Kashmir's constitutional position changed in 2019. Parliament legislated. The President exercised constitutional powers. Article 370 ceased to operate in its previous form. The constitutional foundation upon which Article 35A operated disappeared. The former State was reorganised. The Constitution of India became applicable without the earlier Article 370 framework. And in December 2023, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld the central constitutional result while rejecting the proposition that J&K possessed separate internal sovereignty. These developments cannot be erased by political resolution. That does not mean autonomy cannot be discussed. In a democracy, political parties can advocate constitutional amendments and changes in governmental structure. Even constitutional arrangements that do not presently exist may be proposed politically. But that is fundamentally different from treating the 2000 resolution as though its constitutional premises continue unchanged. Any contemporary autonomy proposal must now answer: What is the constitutional mechanism for achieving it after 2019? Without identifying that mechanism, the autonomy demand remains an expression of political ideology rather than an immediately operative constitutional programme. Separateness Versus Integration The historical debate over autonomy should therefore be understood with precision. The National Conference has maintained that autonomy was intended to preserve J&K's distinctive identity while remaining within India. Critics have argued that the very institutionalisation of constitutional distinctiveness contributed to a politics of separateness and provided narratives that separatist organisations could exploit. These competing interpretations form part of J&K's political history. But post-2019, another consideration has become paramount. The constitutional framework itself has changed. The old argument cannot simply resume from where it stood in 2000. Twenty-six years have passed. Parliament has acted. The constitutional position has changed. The Supreme Court has pronounced upon Article 370. J&K's institutional structure has been reorganised. The constitutional discussion must therefore begin from present constitutional reality rather than historical aspiration. The Constitutional Clock Cannot Simply Be Turned Back Jammu and Kashmir has travelled through several distinct constitutional phases: accession, Article 370, progressive extension of provisions of the Constitution of India, demands for greater autonomy, the 2000 Autonomy Resolution, the constitutional transformation of August 2019 and the Supreme Court judgment of December 2023. History can be debated. Political decisions can be criticised. Constitutional amendments can be advocated. But the constitutional clock cannot simply be reset to 1953 through a resolution of the present Legislative Assembly. The National Conference remains entitled within democratic politics to advocate constitutional change. Its opponents remain equally entitled to argue that the autonomy model perpetuated constitutional exceptionalism and encouraged a politics of separateness. But neither proposition changes the present distribution of constitutional authority. The fundamental question today is therefore no longer merely: “How much autonomy should Jammu and Kashmir have?” The logically prior question is: “What constitutional authority exists today to recreate the pre-2019 arrangement, and through what lawful constitutional mechanism could that authority be exercised?” That is the question created by August 2019 and reinforced by the Supreme Court judgment of December 2023. The present Legislative Assembly can debate aspirations. It can demand restoration of statehood. It can make recommendations to the Union. Political parties can campaign for future constitutional changes. But a legislature functioning within the post-2019 framework cannot, merely through its own resolution, recreate the constitutional order that preceded that framework. The distinction between the democratic freedom to advocate constitutional change and the constitutional authority to effect constitutional change is fundamental. Autonomy may therefore continue as a political idea. But any attempt to present the 2000 formula as a presently available constitutional arrangement must confront Parliament's actions of 2019, the disappearance of the earlier Article 370 framework and the binding constitutional position declared by the Supreme Court. That is why the debate in 2026 cannot simply return to 2000. The constitutional ground beneath it has changed. (The Author is the Chief Spokesperson of JK BJP)

sentences.text: And in December 2023, a Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court upheld the central constitutional result while rejecting the proposition that J&K possessed separate internal sovereignty.

The real question today is consequently more precise: Can the political concept underlying the Autonomy Resolution of 2000 simply be revived after Parliament fundamentally changed J&K's constitutional position in 2019 and the Supreme Court subsequently upheld the central constitutional outcome of those changes?

The Constitutional Clock Cannot Simply Be Turned Back Jammu and Kashmir has travelled through several distinct constitutional phases: accession, Article 370, progressive extension of provisions of the Constitution of India, demands for greater autonomy, the 2000 Autonomy Resolution, the constitutional transformation of August 2019 and the Supreme Court judgment of December 2023.
The 2000 resolution sought restoration of a constitutional arrangement broadly associated with the position existing before 9 August 1953.

stories.headline: KCC&I honours Sheikh Ashiq with lifetime award
stories.title: KCC&I honours Sheikh Ashiq with lifetime award
stories.summary: Srinagar, September 26: The Kashmir Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KCC&I) has honoured its former president Sheikh Ashiq Ahmad with a Lifetime Achievement Award for his longstanding contribution to the business community of Jammu and Kashmir. The award was presented during the Chamber’s 92nd Annual General Meeting held at Taj Dal View, Kralsangri, Srinagar, on Saturday. The recognition acknowledges Sheikh Ashiq’s years of association with KCC&I and his role in raising issues concerning trade, commerce, handicrafts, tourism, industry and exports. During the 2014 Kashmir floods, when businesses and livelihoods suffered extensive losses, Sheikh Ashiq, as KCC&I president, sought rehabilitation and compensation for affected traders and households. The Chamber also approached the Jammu and Kashmir High Court through a Public Interest Litigation seeking directions for the settlement of insurance claims and immediate release of 50 per cent of insured amounts to affected policyholders. According to figures cited by Sheikh Ashiq and reported at the time, insurance companies subsequently disbursed around ₹2,500 crore in flood-related claims. In February 2015, KCC&I also met a visiting World Bank team, presenting assessments of losses across horticulture, agriculture, retail, wholesale, tourism and other sectors and seeking institutional support for economic reconstruction. The Chamber also advocated greater assistance following the announcement of a ₹1,667-crore short-term rehabilitation package, stating that additional support was needed considering the scale of the damage. Sheikh Ashiq continued to raise concerns over the economic difficulties faced by Kashmir’s business community after 2019 and during the COVID-19 period. KCC&I estimated economic losses at around ₹10,000 crore after August 2019 and later revised the estimate to approximately ₹40,000 crore by August 2020. Following representations by the Chamber, the J&K administration constituted a committee in August 2020 to examine economic revival and support for businesses. In September that year, the administration announced a ₹1,350-crore economic package, including a 5 per cent interest subvention for borrowers. Sheikh Ashiq also remained associated with efforts to promote Kashmir’s handicrafts, carpets and export sector. As a member of the Committee of Administration of the Carpet Export Promotion Council, he advocated improved export infrastructure, support for artisans and exporters, and greater market access for Kashmiri handicrafts. KCC&I also raised issues such as high transportation costs and the absence of a dry port before parliamentary committees, while seeking freight support and measures to strengthen the handicraft and carpet industry. The Chamber said the Lifetime Achievement Award recognises Sheikh Ashiq’s sustained representation of traders, exporters, artisans, tourism stakeholders, industrialists and entrepreneurs before government and other institutions. It said the honour was a recognition of his contribution to the organised business community and the institution of KCC&I over the years.

stories.headline: 1,469 JJM schemes completed in J&K
stories.title: 1,469 JJM schemes completed in J&K
stories.summary: Srinagar, Sept 26: As many as 1,469 schemes under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) have been physically completed across Jammu and Kashmir, of which 1,379 have been made operational, the J&K Jal Shakti Department has informed the Legislative Assembly. The department’s response to an unstarred question raised by MLA Sunil Kumar Sharma stated that the remaining 90 schemes are yet to become operational, mainly due to minor connection and commissioning works. Some schemes have also been affected by damage caused during recent floods. The government said the Jal Jeevan Mission is aimed at providing reliable piped drinking-water supply to rural households across Jammu and Kashmir. According to the official reply, the Union Territory utilised ₹5,368.16 crore under the mission during the last three financial years. The expenditure stood at ₹3,875.47 crore in 2023-24, ₹1,478.01 crore in 2024-25, and ₹14.68 crore in 2025-26, The department also provided district-wise details of household tap-water connections. Across Jammu and Kashmir, the data covers 6,251 villages and 19,24,646 households. Of these, 5,75,456 households had tap-water connections as of August 15, 2019, while the total number of household tap connections as on date is 15,66,716. The district-wise figures show considerable expansion in household tap-water coverage across both Jammu and Kashmir divisions under the mission. The Jal Shakti Department further said that the reliable and regular supply of piped drinking water depends on the completion of various schemes sanctioned under the Jal Jeevan Mission and the release of funds by the Central Government and the Union Territory administration. The department said the Government of India has extended the Jal Jeevan Mission up to December 2028, and expressed that all villages in Jammu and Kashmir are expected to have adequate, reliable and regular piped drinking-water supply upon completion of the mission.
